sentences.en: My name is Luca.

sentences.de: Ho ventotto anni e abito a Roma.
sentences.en: I am twenty-eight years old and I live in Rome.
sentences.note: Italian uses avere (to have) for age, not essere.

sentences.en: I have a sister, Sofia.
Sofia is nice and intelligent.
sentences.note: Adjectives ending in -e (intelligente) don't change for gender.

sentences.en: Today is Monday.
It is seven in the morning.
sentences.note: Time uses sono (plural) for any hour after 1.

sentences.de: Mi alzo e vado in cucina.
sentences.en: I get up and go to the kitchen.
I make a strong coffee.

sentences.de: Il caffè è la mia passione.
sentences.en: Coffee is my passion.
sentences.note: Definite article il for masculine; possessive la mia agrees with feminine passione.

sentences.de: Mangio anche un cornetto con marmellata.
sentences.en: I also eat a croissant with jam.

sentences.de: La mia casa è piccola ma luminosa.
sentences.en: My house is small but bright.
sentences.note: Feminine adjectives end in -a: piccola, luminosa.

sentences.de: Ha una camera, un bagno e un soggiorno.
sentences.en: It has a bedroom, a bathroom and a living room.

sentences.de: Dalla finestra vedo i tetti rossi di Roma.
sentences.en: From the window I see the red roofs of Rome.
sentences.note: Contracted preposition: da + la = dalla. Plural masculine adjective: rossi.

sentences.en: At eight I go to work.
sentences.note: Contracted: a + le = alle, a + il = al.

sentences.de: Lavoro in una libreria nel centro.
sentences.en: I work in a bookstore in the center.

sentences.de: Il mio capo si chiama Marco.
sentences.en: My boss is called Marco.
He is kind but strict.
I like my work.
sentences.note: Piacere construction: 'mi piace X' = 'X is pleasing to me'.

sentences.de: A pranzo mangio con la mia collega Giulia.
sentences.en: At lunch I eat with my colleague Giulia.
Giulia is young and funny.
She talks a lot and laughs often.
sentences.note: Regular -are parlare → parla. Irregular ridere → ride.

sentences.en: I eat pasta with tomato sauce.
We drink sparkling water.
sentences.note: L' before vowel; -iamo is the 1st person plural ending.

sentences.en: Lunch is always delicious.

sentences.de: Nel pomeriggio leggo i libri nuovi.
sentences.en: In the afternoon I read the new books.
sentences.note: Plural masculine agreement: i libri nuovi.

sentences.en: At six I return home.
I listen to Italian music.
sentences.note: Adjective italiana agrees with feminine la musica.

sentences.de: La musica è bella e rilassante.
sentences.en: The music is beautiful and relaxing.

sentences.de: La sera leggo o guardo un film.
sentences.en: In the evening I read or watch a film.

sentences.de: Domani è un altro giorno bellissimo.
sentences.en: Tomorrow is another beautiful day.
sentences.note: Suffix -issimo intensifies an adjective: bello → bellissimo.

vocabulary.note: Invariable plural — accent makes it un-changing.
Same form for m. and f. (article changes).
Irregular. io sono, tu sei, lui/lei è, noi siamo, voi siete, loro sono.
Irregular. io ho, tu hai, lui/lei ha, noi abbiamo, voi avete, loro hanno.
Regular -are. parlo, parli, parla, parliamo, parlate, parlano.
Regular -are. Stem -i drops in some forms: mangiamo, mangiate.
Irregular. bevo, bevi, beve, beviamo, bevete, bevono.
Irregular. vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno.
Irregular. faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno.

Reflexive. mi alzo, ti alzi, si alza.
Used with indirect objects: 'mi piace' = I like it (lit. it pleases me).
Also a noun for Italian speaker.
Days of the week are masculine.

grammarRules.name: Essere vs Avere
grammarRules.desc: Italian has two verbs that English speakers often confuse. Use essere (to be) for identity, location, characteristics. Use avere (to have) for possession AND for states English expresses with 'to be' — age, hunger, thirst, cold.
grammarRules.longExplanation: English uses 'to be' for many things — age, hunger, thirst, fear. Italian uses 'avere' (to have) for those instead. So 'I am 28' becomes literally 'I have 28 years' — Ho 28 anni. Use ESSERE only for identity, location, and traits.
tips: Use AVERE for: age, hunger, thirst, cold, hot, fear, need.
Use ESSERE for: identity, location, traits (tall, kind), feelings (happy, sad).

table.title: essere vs avere — present tense
table.note: Both are highly irregular. The 'h' in avere forms is silent.

grammarRules.name: Definite Articles
grammarRules.desc: il (masc. sg.), la (fem. sg.), lo (masc. sg. before s+consonant or z), l' (before vowel), i (masc. pl.), le (fem. pl.), gli (masc. pl. before vowel/s+consonant/z).
grammarRules.longExplanation: Italian definite articles depend on TWO things: gender (masculine/feminine) AND the first letter of the next word. Most words use simple il (m.) and la (f.), but masculine words starting with s+consonant or z take lo, and any word starting with a vowel takes l'.
tips: Masculine: il / lo / l' (sg.), i / gli (pl.).
First letter sound matters: s+consonant or z → lo/gli; vowel → l'.

table.title: Definite articles — singular & plural
table.note: Listen to the first letter SOUND, not just the spelling.

grammarRules.name: Regular -are Verbs
grammarRules.desc: abitare, parlare, lavorare conjugate predictably: -o, -i, -a, -iamo, -ate, -ano. e.g. abitare → abito, abiti, abita, abitiamo, abitate, abitano.
grammarRules.longExplanation: Italian -are verbs are the most regular family. Drop the -are ending and add: -o (I), -i (you), -a (he/she), -iamo (we), -ate (you all), -ano (they). Once you learn this pattern, you can conjugate hundreds of verbs.
tips: Same pattern for: abitare, lavorare, mangiare, ascoltare, guardare.

table.title: Regular -are conjugation: parlare (to speak)
table.note: Stress falls on the second-to-last syllable in most forms — except loro (parlano).

grammarRules.name: Adjective Agreement
grammarRules.desc: Adjectives match the noun's gender and number. -o adjectives: rosso (m.sg.), rossa (f.sg.), rossi (m.pl.), rosse (f.pl.). -e adjectives: gentile / gentili (only 2 forms).
grammarRules.longExplanation: Italian adjectives change endings to match the noun's gender (masculine or feminine) and number (singular or plural). The most common pattern is -o/-a/-i/-e (rosso, rossa, rossi, rosse). Adjectives ending in -e have only two forms: -e (singular) and -i (plural).
tips: -e adjectives have 2 forms (gentile/gentili — no gender distinction).
Adjective comes AFTER the noun in most cases (libro rosso, not 'rosso libro').

table.title: Adjective endings
table.note: -o family has 4 distinct forms; -e family has just 2.

grammarRules.name: Contracted Prepositions
grammarRules.desc: Prepositions a, di, da, in, su contract with the definite article: a+il=al, a+la=alla, di+il=del, da+la=dalla, in+il=nel, etc.
grammarRules.longExplanation: When the prepositions a, di, da, in, su come before the definite article (il, la, le, etc.), they merge into a single word. You almost never say 'a il' — it becomes 'al'. Memorize the most common ones: al, alla, alle, del, della, dal, dalla, nel, nella.
tips: 5 prepositions × 7 articles = ~35 contractions, but most are predictable.
If you say 'a il' or 'di il', it sounds wrong to native ears — it's always contracted.

table.title: Preposition + article contractions
table.note: con, per, tra/fra do NOT contract — they stay as separate words.

grammarTests.trap: Italian uses avere for cold, hunger, thirst, age — literally 'I have cold'.
Both adjectives need feminine plural -e endings.
a + il = al (one word, not 'a il').
